title.value: What We Do in the Shadows

logline: A mockumentary crew films four vampire flatmates and their energy-vampire familiar living in Staten Island, New York - one of the funniest and most consistently inventive comedies of the 2020s.

bollymeter.basis: Universally acclaimed debut that successfully transplanted the 2014 NZ film mockumentary format to a US network context while adding new comic registers through Harvey Guillen's Guillermo.

seasons.review_body: Season 1 premiered March 27, 2019, transplanting Taika Waititi and Jemaine Clement’s 2014 New Zealand mockumentary film to Staten Island. Showrunner Paul Simms built the series around three ancient European vampires Nandor (Kayvan Novak), Laszlo (Matt Berry), and Nadja (Natasia Demetriou), alongside their energy-vampire flatmate Colin Robinson (Mark Proksch), whose supernatural power drains life through boring conversation. Harvey Guillen as Guillermo de la Cruz, Nandor’s human familiar who secretly descends from vampire hunters, became the emotional centre. The show maintains a deadpan mock-doc commitment while extending the film’s joke structure into a serialised format without grinding down the premise.

episode_reviews.spoiler_free: What We Do in the Shadows' FX series premiere transplants Taika Waititi and Jemaine Clement's mockumentary vampire format from New Zealand to Staten Island. The American adaptation establishes its register immediately - the Staten Island housemateship of four ancient vampires being documented by a camera crew - and proves that the premise is more elastic than its feature film origin suggested. Kayvan Novak's Nandor the Relentless and Matt Berry's Laszlo are fully formed comic instruments in the pilot.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The Staten Island vampire council meeting - the episode's comic escalation that demonstrates the series' ability to find absurdity in vampire mythology without condescending to it.
episode_reviews.review_body:
# What We Do In The Shadows S01E01: "Pilot" Review

*Spoiler-light verdict above. Full episode analysis below.*

The casket opens, and **Baron Afanas** eats a familiar. That is the pilot's cleanest statement of intent. The vampires spend the episode building rules around a visit they cannot control, then the old power arrives and treats their planning like garnish. A black van. A blood feast. A special plan. A letter read with ceremonial nonsense. All of it meets appetite. "Pilot" works because it treats vampire tradition as administration, then lets one ancient monster remind the room that the paperwork was never the point.

## Protocol Is the First Punchline

The episode begins with **Guillermo** confirming his role as **Nandor**'s familiar and announcing that it is time to rise. That small act of service gives the pilot its engine. The household runs on routine before it runs on power. Someone wakes them. Someone gathers them. Someone keeps the undead calendar from becoming a mess.

Then **Laszlo** insists on reading the received letter in the library as a formality. The joke goes beyond vampires being old-fashioned. They adore procedure even when procedure solves nothing. By the time they close the door and gather under invented protocols, the pilot has found its comic shape: these creatures have eternity and still manage to turn a letter into a meeting that could have been shorter.

That is strong pilot writing because it sells the hierarchy through behavior. Guillermo is useful, Nandor is the gravitational center, Laszlo can make ceremony feel important, and the group can turn any task into theater. The supernatural world arrives through chores. That is where the hour gets its bite. It lets them build a ritual around an envelope.

The risk is visible too. Protocol comedy can flatten if the only gag is delay. The pilot dodges that by making the letter matter: Baron Afanas is coming tomorrow. Suddenly the nonsense has a deadline.

## The Black Van Plan Has No Adult in the Room

Nandor responds to the Baron's impending arrival with a plan: a black van and virgins. That is the episode's best kind of stupid because it is specific. The goal is practical in the vampires' minds. They need transportation, victims, and the visit to look like competence. The comedy comes from the gap between how serious the plan sounds inside the house and how shabby it feels as logistics.

Nandor wants the visit to go smoothly, with virgins ready for a blood feast. He proceeds as if planning creates control. The pilot keeps making ritual crash into execution. A formal letter can be read. A protocol can be invented. A van can be imagined. None of that means the night will obey.

This is where the episode's structure starts doing more than introducing characters. The Baron's arrival becomes the pressure test. Every earlier habit, from ceremony to delegation, has to survive contact with an actual event. The vampires want to appear ancient and fearsome, but the hour keeps dragging them back into the management problem of hosting. In an Indian family comedy, this would be the wedding house panicking before the baraat. Here the baraat is an ancient vampire in a casket, and the catering is blood.

The joke lands because the plan fits them exactly: theatrical, immoral, undercooked.

## Colin Robinson Turns Failure Into a Skill

**Colin Robinson** identifies himself as a psychic, energy vampire, and the pilot immediately understands his value. He is the least visually grand figure in a room built around gothic posturing, which makes him the perfect saboteur. The others drain blood. He drains patience. More important, he drains the episode's logistics.

When Colin drains the virgins of energy, the visit's machinery begins to collapse from inside the plan. This is the pilot's smartest escalation. The disaster does not come from a heroic outsider or a sudden moral obstacle. It comes from a housemate doing exactly what he wants to do. Colin is a character contradiction made operational.

That gives the comedy a nasty edge. The vampires can handle danger in theory. They cannot handle a colleague whose talent is making everyone weaker by talking. The show places him beside grand vampire mythology and refuses to separate office irritation from supernatural threat. That collision is the point.

It is also the episode's strongest character introduction. Guillermo gives the story duty. Nandor gives it delusion. Laszlo gives it ceremony. Colin gives it drag, in the funniest sense: he slows the blood feast by being himself. The one limitation is that the beat is more functional than surprising. Once his power is defined, the virgins becoming unusable is an almost too-clean payoff. For a pilot, the simplicity works. The audience needs the rules fast, and the episode does not waste the lesson.

## The Baron Eats the Plan

When Baron Afanas's casket opens and a familiar is eaten, the pilot shifts from household farce to consequence without changing its comic skin. That matters. The episode has spent its time making the vampires look silly, but the Baron's appetite brings danger back into the room. It is a correction: these people may be incompetent hosts, yet the world they belong to can still kill casually.

The proclamation that follows gives the visit weight. The New World is declared their lifeline, which turns the Baron's arrival from a social obligation into a mission statement. The pilot plants its season question there. What happens when a group built for delay is asked to act with purpose? The household can perform respect. It can perform order. The Baron demands more than performance.

This is also where the pacing tightens. The earlier scenes stretch protocol and preparation. The Baron sequence compresses the result: casket, hunger, proclamation. The rhythm shows the difference between the vampires who live in the house and the power that has come to judge them. Nandor and the others talk themselves into structure. The Baron arrives and changes the room by opening his mouth.

The turn could use one more beat of dread before the familiar is eaten. The pilot is designed for speed, and that speed keeps the comedy crisp, but the horror would land harder with a little more room. The scene still does the job. It makes the old ways feel less like costume and more like a threat with teeth.

## Guillermo Gets the Gift, and the Gag Gets the Last Word

The episode saves Guillermo's anniversary for the closing move, and it is smart placement. After all the attention on the Baron's visit, the household's biggest personal debt is to the person doing the work. Guillermo wants to fulfill his duties and prepare for Nandor's plans. Nandor appears to have a special plan for him. The payoff is a glitter portrait.

That is a perfect dumb object for a milestone. The glitter portrait undercuts the grandeur Guillermo wants without erasing his desire. The pilot understands that his loyalty needs recognition, then refuses to make the recognition majestic. This is the show's basic bargain in miniature: the myth will be honored, then made tacky.

The long silence near the end is a bold tonal kink. After dense comic dialogue and rapid role switching, nearly a minute of quiet creates a hard drop before the episode closes. It is abrupt by design, though not perfectly smooth. The silence makes the ending feel less like a conventional button and more like the air leaking out of a room after too much ceremony. The instinct is stronger than the execution. The gap is memorable, but it slightly blunts the immediate comic momentum of Guillermo's gift.

Still, the closing beat puts the pilot's thesis in one image. Guillermo wants elevation. Nandor gives him elevation by way of glitter. Eternal life, apparently, still has arts and crafts.

## The Verdict

"Pilot" is a sharp first outing because it builds a vampire comedy around process failure. The episode's best idea is that ancient power looks funniest when it has to host, schedule, delegate, and improvise. Laszlo's formality, Nandor's undercooked plan, Colin Robinson's energy drain, and Baron Afanas's brutal arrival all serve the same argument: ceremony can fill a room, but appetite decides the night. The hour has a few rough seams, especially in how quickly the Baron sequence moves and how abruptly the closing silence lands. Even so, the character functions are clear, the gags come from behavior, and the season's larger question is planted cleanly. If this is the house's normal level of competence, the Baron's New World demand is less a mission than a stress test.

Written by BollyAI, reviewed by our editorial team.

verdict.one_liner: A sharp pilot where vampire ceremony keeps collapsing into office-level logistics, with one rushed gift that still lands.

bollymeter.basis: Season 2 deepened the Guillermo arc while expanding the world-building; critics and audiences considered it a step up from an already strong debut.

seasons.review_body: Season 2 aired April 2020 and is the point at which the series found its fullest voice. The Guillermo storyline, his ancestry as a Van Helsing descendant, was developed more explicitly, giving the show a genuine emotional throughline beneath the deadpan humour. Matt Berry's Laszlo emerged as a standout character, with his particular brand of oblivious aristocratic idiocy generating some of the season's best material. The writing carries confidence, and the supernatural world expands in a way that keeps building quietly rather than announcing itself. Season 2 demonstrates that the mockumentary format can sustain long-form character work without sacrificing its core comic timing.
seasons.season_over_season: Deepens character work beneath the deadpan surface; Guillermo's ancestry and Laszlo's comedic register emerge as the show's structural pillars.

bollymeter.basis: Peaked creatively in the view of many critics; the energy-vampire plotline reached its most ambitious point and the ensemble dynamic was at its most precisely calibrated.

seasons.review_body: Season 3 arrived September 2021 and stands as the series' creative peak. The Colin Robinson energy-vampire storyline developed into territory that requires genuine dramatic investment alongside the comedy, and the ensemble chemistry is at its most precisely calibrated across the ten episodes. Guest casting and the expansion of the supernatural world-building both hit their marks. This season also marks the point where the show outgrows its film-adaptation origins, taking on a distinct identity and bigger ambitions.
seasons.season_over_season: The ensemble and its world reach maximum creative coherence, and the series hits its artistic peak.

bollymeter.basis: Critical enthusiasm remained strong but discourse noted the show beginning to settle into its own formulas; still among the best comedies on television but the unpredictability of peak seasons reduced.

seasons.review_body: Season 4 aired July 2022 and remained a critical and audience favourite while discourse began noting that the show was working within increasingly familiar parameters. The ensemble remained exceptional and individual episodes still produced genuinely memorable set pieces. Critics acknowledged the slight diminishment from Season 3's peak without suggesting the show had declined significantly - the baseline quality of What We Do in the Shadows was simply high enough that 'settling' still meant better than most comedies on television.
seasons.season_over_season: Comfortable and accomplished rather than surprising; the show's mastery of its own form now reads as confidence rather than novelty.

bollymeter.basis: Consistent quality maintained but critical conversation had largely moved on; the show's late-career run rewarded loyal viewers more than it attracted new critical attention.

seasons.review_body: Season 5 aired July 2023 as the penultimate run. Critical coverage remained positive but less intensive than the show's peak years. The writing maintained the series' standards and the ensemble continued to find new comic business within familiar structures. Season 5 functioned largely as setup for the final season's character resolutions, and reviewers who engaged with it deeply found it rewarding; those expecting a creative resurgence from the post-season-3 trajectory were not surprised to find the show in a comfortable late-career mode.
seasons.season_over_season: Penultimate season that seeds conclusions without delivering them; competent and warm but not revelatory.

bollymeter.basis: The finale season earned credit for landing the character arcs - particularly Guillermo's - in a way that respected six years of investment, even if the final episode was more elegiac than conclusive.

seasons.review_body: Season 6 concluded December 16, 2024 across eleven episodes. The extra runtime gave the writers room to resolve the series' central relationships. Guillermo's arc across six seasons stands out as one of the most sustained character journeys in recent prestige comedy, and the finale’s handling of his story drives much of the season’s takeaway. The series resists a tidy resolution while still finding emotional closure for its characters. It ends with a calm, appreciative finish that underscores the show’s strengths without leaning on manufactured urgency.
seasons.season_over_season: The series finale delivers on the Guillermo arc and closes the show on its own terms; a graceful rather than spectacular ending.
